questions.question_text:
A cyclist moves in the positive direction along a straight road. The cyclist's velocity is measured at the following times.

| $t$ (seconds) | $0$ | $1$ | $2$ | $3$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $v$ (m/s) | $2$ | $5$ | $8$ | $11$ |

Using the trapezoidal rule, what is the estimated distance travelled in the first $3$ seconds?

options.why: Did not double the interior velocities: $\frac12(2+5+8+11)=13$.
Omitted the factor $\frac12$ from the trapezoidal rule.
Multiplied the final velocity $11\text{ m/s}$ by $3$ seconds, treating the velocity as constant.

questions.solution_text:
The velocity is nonnegative, so the area under the velocity–time graph gives distance.
$h=1$
Distance $\approx\frac12\left(2+11+2(5+8)\right)$
$=\frac12(39)$
$=19.5\text{ m}$

options.why: Added the final rate $15+4(6)=39$ to the initial $100$ litres instead of integrating the rate.
Integrated only the constant term $15$, giving $90$ litres added, then added the initial $100$ litres.
Multiplied the final rate $39$ litres per minute by $6$ minutes, then added the initial $100$ litres.

questions.solution_text:
The volume added is the area under the rate–time graph.
Volume added $=\int_{0}^{6}(15+4t)\,dt$
$=\left[15t+2t^{2}\right]_{0}^{6}$
$=90+72$
$=162\text{ L}$
Final volume $=100+162=262\text{ L}$

options.why: Integrated only from $x=0$ to $x=2$, so only half of the symmetric cross-section was counted.
Correct value, but a region bounded by two lengths in metres has an area in $\text{m}^{2}$, not a volume.
Used only half the cross-section and also gave cubic metres instead of square metres.

questions.question_text:
A lake's widths are measured at $8$-metre intervals along a straight baseline.

| Distance along baseline (m) | $0$ | $8$ | $16$ | $24$ | $32$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Width (m) | $0$ | $12$ | $18$ | $10$ | $0$ |

Using the trapezoidal rule, what is the estimated surface area of the lake?

options.why: Did not double the interior widths: $\frac82(12+18+10)=160$.
Omitted the factor $\frac12$ from the trapezoidal rule.
Treated the lake as a rectangle with its maximum width $18$ metres and length $32$ metres.

questions.question_text:
A reservoir initially contains $100$ megalitres of water. Its net inflow rate is $R=8-3t$ megalitres per day, for $0\leq t\leq4$ days. A negative rate means water is being released.
What volume is in the reservoir after $4$ days?

options.why: Reported only the net change and did not add the initial $100\text{ ML}$.
Subtracted the positive net change $8\text{ ML}$ from the initial volume instead of adding it.
Used the final rate $-4\text{ ML/day}$ for all $4$ days, giving $100+4(-4)=84$.

questions.solution_text:
Net change $=\int_0^4(8-3t)\,dt$
$=\left[8t-\frac32t^2\right]_0^4$
$=32-24$
$=8\text{ ML}$
Final volume $=100+8=108\text{ ML}$

questions.question_text:
A tank initially contains $400$ litres of water. A pump delivers water at a rate of $R=9t^2$ litres per second, for $0\leq t\leq4$ seconds.
How much water is in the tank after $4$ seconds?

options.why: Reported only the water delivered and omitted the initial $400$ litres.
Added the final rate $9(4)^2=144$ to the initial volume instead of integrating the rate.
Multiplied the final rate $144$ litres per second by $4$ seconds, then added the initial volume.

questions.solution_text:
Volume added $=\int_0^4 9t^2\,dt$
$=\left[3t^3\right]_0^4$
$=192\text{ L}$
Final volume $=400+192=592\text{ L}$

options.why: Left out the factor $\frac{1}{0.2}$ in the primitive, then subtracted the resulting loss $500(1-e^{-1})$ from $3000$ kL and rounded.
Used $2500$ kL as the loss by omitting the upper-limit term, then calculated $3000-2500=500$ kL.
Treated the final rate as constant for all $5$ days, then calculated $3000-5(500e^{-1})$ and rounded.
Integrated only from $0$ to $\frac{\pi}{2}$, taking half the symmetric region.
Correct value, but a region bounded by two lengths in metres has an area in $\text{m}^{2}$.
Used only half the region and also gave cubic metres instead of square metres.

questions.question_text:
A tank initially contains $200$ litres of water. Water flows into it at a rate of $R=6\sqrt{t}$ litres per hour, for $0\leq t\leq9$ hours.
What volume is in the tank after $9$ hours?

options.why: Reported only the volume added and omitted the initial $200$ litres.
Multiplied the final rate $18$ litres per hour by $9$ hours, then added the initial volume.
Added the final rate $6\sqrt9=18$ to the initial volume instead of integrating the rate.

questions.solution_text:
Volume added $=\int_0^9 6t^{\frac12}\,dt$
$=\left[4t^{\frac32}\right]_0^9$
$=4(27)$
$=108\text{ L}$
Final volume $=200+108=308\text{ L}$
